title: GMAT Focus Verbal Practice Test 6
instructions: Original exam-style practice test with answers and explanations.

questions.prompt: An airline introduced a charge for checked baggage and reports that the average time its aircraft spend at the gate between flights has fallen. It attributes the improvement to passengers carrying fewer checked bags, which speeds loading.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the airline's attribution?
options: A. Some passengers pay the charge without complaint.
B. Baggage handlers report that the work is easier than before.
C. The airline simultaneously introduced a boarding procedure that seats passengers by row, and gate times fell equally on routes where checked baggage did not decline.
D. Competing airlines charge similar fees.
E. The charge raised more revenue than forecast.
questions.explanation: A concurrent change that produced the same effect where the proposed cause was absent is the strongest available challenge. C is consistent with the airline's account rather than against it.

questions.prompt: A restaurant group replaced tipping with a service charge included in menu prices, and reports that staff turnover has fallen by half. The group concludes that predictable pay is what servers value most.
questions.question: The conclusion is most vulnerable to the criticism that it
options: A. ignores the preferences of customers
B. fails to specify the size of the service charge
C. does not consider the group's profitability
D. assumes that turnover is a reliable indicator of staff satisfaction rather than of conditions in the wider labour market
E. relies on data from a single year
questions.explanation: Turnover falls when outside opportunities dry up, whatever the employer does; without a comparison the inference about what servers value is unsupported. B and D are real considerations but do not bear on the causal claim.

questions.prompt: A seed company found that fields sown with its new drought-tolerant wheat variety yielded more than neighbouring fields sown with the standard variety during a dry season, and advertises the new variety as higher-yielding.
questions.question: Which of the following would be most useful to determine in evaluating the advertisement?
options: A. How much the new seed costs per hectare
B. Whether the new variety yields as well as the standard variety in seasons of normal rainfall
C. Whether the fields were of similar size
D. How many farmers have purchased the new variety
E. Whether the company conducted the comparison itself
questions.explanation: The claim is unqualified, so what matters is performance across conditions: drought tolerance is frequently traded against yield in good years. B and E bear on value and credibility, not on whether the claim is true.

questions.prompt: A public library replaced part of its printed stock with e-book licences and reports that total loans rose. The head librarian concludes that readers prefer e-books.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most seriously undermines the conclusion?
options: A. E-book licences expire after a fixed number of loans.
B. Some readers do not own suitable devices.
C. The library extended its opening hours in the same period.
D. Printed loans fell slightly.
E. Each e-book licence permits several simultaneous borrowers, so titles that previously had waiting lists are now always available.
questions.explanation: Availability, not preference, can explain the rise: loans that were previously suppressed by queues now complete. D offers a rival cause but a weaker one, since it would raise printed loans too.

questions.prompt: Every car park in the Ashcombe district that charges by the hour is monitored by camera. No car park monitored by camera has been the site of a reported theft this year. Some car parks in the district charge a flat daily rate.
questions.question: If the statements above are true, which of the following must be true?
options: A. No car park that charges by the hour has been the site of a reported theft this year.
B. No car park in the district has been the site of a reported theft this year.
C. Car parks charging a flat daily rate are not monitored by camera.
D. Most car parks in the district charge by the hour.
E. Cameras deter theft.
questions.explanation: Hourly implies camera implies no reported theft. A goes too far, since flat-rate car parks may be unmonitored; C wrongly denies the antecedent; E is a causal claim the statements do not support.

questions.prompt: A factory introduced a scheme under which workers report near-misses anonymously. In the first year, reported near-misses rose sharply while recorded injuries fell. A manager concludes that the factory has become more dangerous but that workers are being more careful.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, best explains the pattern the manager describes?
options: A. The factory hired additional workers during the year.
B. Injuries are recorded by an external inspector.
C. Near-misses were previously under-reported because workers feared blame, and the anonymous scheme captures events that were always occurring.
D. The scheme was publicised widely within the factory.
E. Some near-misses involve equipment that has since been replaced.
questions.explanation: A change in reporting explains a rise in reports without any rise in hazards, which removes the manager's paradox. D explains awareness of the scheme but not the divergence between the two measures.

questions.prompt: A conservation group argues that salmon farms should be moved away from river mouths, since parasite levels on wild juvenile salmon are far higher near farms than elsewhere.
questions.question: The argument depends on which of the following assumptions?
options: A. Salmon farming is unprofitable at its current locations.
B. Parasites are the main cause of decline in wild salmon numbers.
C. Farms can be relocated without loss of production.
D. Wild salmon do not migrate past the farms twice.
E. The elevated parasite levels near farms are not primarily caused by some feature of river mouths that is independent of the farms.
questions.explanation: The recommendation treats the farms as the source; if river mouths themselves concentrate parasites, moving the farms would not help. C strengthens the case for acting but is not required for the inference that farms are responsible.

questions.prompt: A software firm found that employees hired through referrals from existing staff stay longer than those hired through advertisements. It plans to fill all future vacancies through referrals in order to reduce turnover.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, casts most doubt on the plan?
options: A. Referred candidates are often friends of existing employees.
B. Advertising vacancies is expensive.
C. Some referred employees have left within a year.
D. Referrals draw from a pool similar in background to current staff, and the firm's growth requires skills its current staff do not have.
E. The firm's turnover is lower than the industry average.
questions.explanation: It identifies a cost of the policy that the retention statistic does not capture: a hiring channel that cannot supply the skills needed is a poor way to staff the firm, whatever its retention record.

questions.prompt: A regional government reports that since it began paying for wind turbines, the region's carbon emissions have fallen, and concludes that the turbines caused the reduction.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the conclusion?
options: A. The turbines generate less electricity in summer than in winter.
B. The region's largest steelworks closed in the same period and had accounted for a fifth of regional emissions.
C. Some residents objected to the turbines on visual grounds.
D. Neighbouring regions have also installed turbines.
E. The turbines cost more than projected.
questions.explanation: A single large emitter leaving accounts for the fall without any contribution from the turbines. A limits the size of the effect but does not challenge the causal claim.

questions.prompt: A cheesemaker matures its cheese for eighteen months rather than the usual twelve, and its cheese sells at a premium. A competitor concludes that maturing cheese longer allows any producer to charge more.
questions.question: The competitor's reasoning is flawed because it
options: A. assumes that what holds for one producer with an established reputation will hold for producers generally
B. ignores the cost of storing cheese for longer
C. overlooks differences in milk quality
D. treats price as a measure of quality
E. relies on the testimony of a single cheesemaker
questions.explanation: The premium may attach to the maker's reputation rather than to the ageing, and the inference generalises from one case to all producers. B is a genuine cost but does not identify the reasoning error.

questions.prompt: A city installed cameras to enforce its bus lanes and reports that bus journey times have improved. Opponents argue that the cameras were installed mainly to raise revenue from fines, noting that fine income has exceeded the enforcement budget every year.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most weakens the opponents' argument?
options: A. The city has installed cameras in other locations as well.
B. Bus passenger numbers have increased.
C. Fine income has fallen each year as compliance has risen, and the city's own projections anticipated that decline.
D. Some drivers say the lane markings are unclear.
E. Fines are set at the same level as in neighbouring cities.
questions.explanation: A revenue motive predicts arrangements that sustain income; a declining, and expected to decline, income stream is the signature of an enforcement objective instead. C is consistent with both accounts.

questions.passageText:
A firm with cash it does not need can return it to shareholders by paying a dividend or by buying back its own shares. In a frictionless market the two are equivalent: the shareholder who wants income can sell a portion of a holding, and the shareholder who wants to reinvest can decline to sell. Actual firms treat the choice as consequential, and the reasons lie in the frictions the equivalence assumes away.

The first is the signal each carries. Dividends are treated by managers as a commitment: cutting one is read as evidence of distress, and firms will borrow to avoid it. A buyback carries no such expectation, which makes it the instrument of choice for cash a firm suspects may not recur. Investors, aware of this, read a dividend increase as a stronger statement about future earnings than a buyback of equal value.

The second is who benefits. A buyback raises earnings per share by reducing the denominator, and where executive pay is tied to that figure the interests of managers and shareholders diverge. A firm may repurchase shares at prices its own managers believe are high, transferring value from continuing shareholders to those who sell, and the empirical record on the timing of repurchases is not flattering.

Critics have argued that buybacks divert funds from investment. The evidence is mixed and the argument frequently confuses cause with symptom: firms with attractive projects rarely repurchase shares instead of funding them, and a firm returning cash is often one that has already concluded, rightly or not, that it has nothing better to do with it.
questions.prompt: According to the passage, dividends and buybacks would be equivalent if
options: A. executive pay were not tied to earnings per share
B. managers did not have private information about future earnings
C. tax rates on the two were identical
D. the frictions the equivalence assumes away did not exist
E. firms had no attractive investment projects
questions.explanation: The first paragraph sets up the frictionless equivalence and then says the reasons firms treat the choice as consequential lie in the frictions that equivalence assumes away. A and B name particular frictions but not the general condition.

questions.passageText:
That migratory birds can orient themselves has been established for decades; how they do it remains only partly understood, and the difficulty is instructive about what counts as evidence in sensory biology.

Behavioural experiments established early that birds use several cues. Caged migrants orient in the seasonally appropriate direction under a natural night sky, and shift accordingly when the sky is artificially rotated, which implicates star patterns. Others reorient when placed in an altered magnetic field, which implicates a magnetic sense. Since the cues can conflict, birds must also weigh them, and evidence suggests some species recalibrate their magnetic compass against celestial cues at dusk.

The mechanism of magnetic detection has proved harder. Two candidate systems have dominated. The first involves magnetite, crystals of iron oxide found in tissue, which could transmit force to a sensory cell. The second, radical-pair chemistry, proposes that a light-sensitive protein in the retina forms pairs of molecules whose reaction rates depend on magnetic field orientation, effectively allowing a bird to see direction. That the avian magnetic compass depends on light, and is disrupted by weak radio-frequency fields, fits the second proposal better than the first.

Caution remains warranted. Demonstrating that a candidate molecule is magnetically sensitive in a test tube does not establish that it performs that role in a living bird, and attempts to identify the sensory cells and their neural connections have produced results that have been difficult to replicate. What is secure is the behaviour; what remains open is the machinery, and the gap between the two is wider than popular accounts suggest.
questions.prompt: The experiments involving an artificially rotated night sky are cited to show that
options: A. star patterns are among the cues birds use to orient
B. birds cannot orient without starlight
C. magnetic cues are unimportant in caged birds
D. birds recalibrate their compass at dawn
E. orientation is learned rather than innate
questions.explanation: Caged migrants shifting direction with the rotated sky implicates celestial cues. A overstates — the passage says birds use several cues.

questions.passageText:
The standard measure of unemployment counts a person as unemployed only if they are out of work, available for work, and have actively sought work in a recent reference period. The definition is deliberate rather than arbitrary: without the search requirement, the figure would include people who are not participating in the labour market at all, and would lose its usefulness as an indicator of slack.

The consequence is that the rate can fall for two opposite reasons. People may find jobs, or people may stop looking and be reclassified as outside the labour force. In prolonged downturns the second effect is substantial, and a headline rate that improves while employment does not is a familiar pattern in the historical record.

Statistical agencies address this with supplementary measures. Broader definitions add those who want work but have not searched recently, and those working part-time who would prefer full-time hours. The gap between the narrow and broad measures widens in weak labour markets and narrows in strong ones, which is itself informative.

None of this makes the standard rate a poor measure. It makes it a measure of one thing, and the interpretive error is to treat it as a summary of the labour market as a whole. The most useful reading takes the unemployment rate alongside the employment-to-population ratio and the participation rate, because a movement that all three agree on means something quite different from a movement in the headline rate alone.
questions.prompt: The passage indicates that the search requirement is included in the definition of unemployment in order to
options: A. reduce the cost of collecting labour statistics
B. exclude people who are not participating in the labour market, preserving the figure's use as an indicator of slack
C. make international comparison possible
D. distinguish part-time from full-time workers
E. prevent double counting of the self-employed
questions.explanation: Stated as the deliberate purpose of the requirement in the first paragraph.

options: A. the participation rate rises
B. part-time work is reclassified as full-time
C. the reference period is lengthened
D. employment rises, or because people stop looking for work
E. wages increase

options: A. a measure of one thing, best read alongside the employment ratio and participation rate

questions.passageText:
Hindu-Arabic numerals reached Europe through Arabic mathematical works well before European merchants adopted them. The gap between availability and use is long enough to require explanation, and the usual one — that the new numerals were obviously superior and resistance was mere conservatism — does not survive examination.

Roman numerals were not used for calculation. Arithmetic was performed on a counting board or with an abacus, and the numerals recorded the result. Judged as a notation for recording, they were adequate, and the advantage of the new system appeared only when calculation moved onto paper, which required the algorithms for written multiplication and division that the numerals alone did not supply.

There were also reasons for suspicion that were not superstitious. A written figure can be altered: a zero is easily turned into another digit, and several Italian cities restricted the use of the new numerals in official records for that reason. Roman numerals written out in words in contracts are harder to falsify, and the practice of writing sums in words on cheques descends from the same concern.

Adoption followed the spread of double-entry accounting and of commercial arithmetic teaching, both of which made written calculation routine. The lesson is not that merchants were slow but that a notation is adopted for what it lets its users do, and that the advantage of the new numerals depended on a body of technique that took generations to spread.
questions.prompt: The passage argues that the delay in adopting Hindu-Arabic numerals is not well explained by
options: A. restrictions imposed by Italian cities
B. the spread of commercial arithmetic teaching
C. the claim that the numerals were obviously superior and merchants merely conservative
D. the use of counting boards for arithmetic
E. the difficulty of altering figures written in words
questions.explanation: The first paragraph names that explanation and says it does not survive examination.

What is secure is the behaviour; what remains open is the machinery, and the gap between the two is wider than popular accounts suggest.

readingPassages.title: Counting the Unemployed
readingPassages.text:
The standard measure of unemployment counts a person as unemployed only if they are out of work, available for work, and have actively sought work in a recent reference period. The definition is deliberate rather than arbitrary: without the search requirement, the figure would include people who are not participating in the labour market at all, and would lose its usefulness as an indicator of slack.

The consequence is that the rate can fall for two opposite reasons. People may find jobs, or people may stop looking and be reclassified as outside the labour force. In prolonged downturns the second effect is substantial, and a headline rate that improves while employment does not is a familiar pattern in the historical record.

Statistical agencies address this with supplementary measures. Broader definitions add those who want work but have not searched recently, and those working part-time who would prefer full-time hours. The gap between the narrow and broad measures widens in weak labour markets and narrows in strong ones, which is itself informative.

None of this makes the standard rate a poor measure. It makes it a measure of one thing, and the interpretive error is to treat it as a summary of the labour market as a whole. The most useful reading takes the unemployment rate alongside the employment-to-population ratio and the participation rate, because a movement that all three agree on means something quite different from a movement in the headline rate alone.

readingPassages.title: Numerals and Commerce
readingPassages.text:
Hindu-Arabic numerals reached Europe through Arabic mathematical works well before European merchants adopted them. The gap between availability and use is long enough to require explanation, and the usual one — that the new numerals were obviously superior and resistance was mere conservatism — does not survive examination.

Roman numerals were not used for calculation. Arithmetic was performed on a counting board or with an abacus, and the numerals recorded the result. Judged as a notation for recording, they were adequate, and the advantage of the new system appeared only when calculation moved onto paper, which required the algorithms for written multiplication and division that the numerals alone did not supply.

There were also reasons for suspicion that were not superstitious. A written figure can be altered: a zero is easily turned into another digit, and several Italian cities restricted the use of the new numerals in official records for that reason. Roman numerals written out in words in contracts are harder to falsify, and the practice of writing sums in words on cheques descends from the same concern.

Adoption followed the spread of double-entry accounting and of commercial arithmetic teaching, both of which made written calculation routine. The lesson is not that merchants were slow but that a notation is adopted for what it lets its users do, and that the advantage of the new numerals depended on a body of technique that took generations to spread.
